title: Analytica explicatio methodi maximorum et minimorum

deep.reconstruction:
This is §§XXXII–XXXV of E297 (Novi Commentarii 10, 1764/1766), pp. 114–115. Euler is setting out the formal operational rules of his calculus of variations, which he has rebuilt on Lagrange's δ-notation. Throughout, x is the independent variable and is not varied (δx = 0), so the variation δ acts only through y and through p = dy/dx, q = dp/dx, and so on.

§XXXII: the two operators commute, δdV = dδV. By iteration, δddU = dδdU = ddδU. More generally, any string of d's and a δ can be reordered, e.g. δd³V = dδd²V = d²δdV = d³δV. Because only one varied state is considered (first variation), δ occurs at most once in such a string. Euler recommends always moving δ to the last position.

§XXXIII: variation commutes with integration over the same state, δ∫V = ∫δV. The justification is that the variation of a sum is the sum of the variations of its elements. Applied to the functional, δ∫Z dx = ∫δ(Z dx) = ∫δZ·dx, since δdx = 0 follows from δx = 0. For iterated integrals, δ∫∫V = ∫δ∫V = ∫∫δV. This rule is the tool for the coming case where Z itself contains integral formulas.

§XXXIV: repeated integration by parts, which moves all derivatives off δv. In modern form,
∫V dⁿδv = Σ_{k=0}^{n-1} (−1)^k d^kV · d^{n-1-k}δv + (−1)^n ∫ δv dⁿV.
Euler writes this out explicitly for n = 1 to 4 and indicates the inductive step.

§XXXV: with these rules, every such maximum–minimum problem reduces to computing δ∫Z dx, even when Z contains integral formulas. The next pages carry this out and derive the Euler–Lagrange expression N − dP/dx + ddQ/dx² − … together with the boundary terms.
errors: p.114: 'ob δdU = dδV' should read dδU. Likewise 'si V iam sit differentiale formae dV' should be 'formae dU'. These are notational slips, apparently in the print itself.

The free permutation of d and δ is valid only under Euler's standing assumption that the independent variable is not varied (δx = 0, hence δdx = 0, dx constant). With δx ≠ 0 the commutation fails in general. Euler does not flag this restriction here; it was addressed later, e.g. in his treatments allowing variation of x.

The remark that δ can occur only once restricts the theory to the first variation. Second-variation (sufficiency) questions are thereby excluded; they were taken up later, notably by Legendre in 1786.
On the next page (p.117), the last term of the ∫S d⁴δy expansion is printed with −∫ where it should be +∫. The collected final formula has the correct sign. The p.115 formulas themselves check out.

ideas.what: Commutation of variation and differentiation, δd = dδ, with δx = 0
ideas.modern_name: Commutation of the variation with the derivative (∂/∂ε and d/dx commute)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Lagrange (1755 letter to Euler; Miscellanea Taurinensia 1760–61)

ideas.what: Interchange of variation and integration, including for iterated integrals
ideas.modern_name: Differentiation under the integral sign / linearity of the first variation

ideas.what: General repeated integration-by-parts formula for ∫V dⁿδv
ideas.modern_name: Iterated integration by parts (Leibniz-type formula); source of the boundary terms
ideas.usually_credited_to: Leibniz/Taylor tradition; standard in Lagrange and Euler
ideas.where_published: E296, E297; later Institutiones calculi integralis vol. III appendix (E385)

deep.surprise_reason: These are standard operational rules of the δ-calculus. They are well documented in histories of the calculus of variations (Goldstine, Fraser) and in Euler's companion paper E296. The page contains nothing new.
transcription_corrections: 'ob δ dU = dδ V [?]' — the image shows 'ob δdU = dδV'. It is a printed slip for dδU; the [?] can be removed with that note.
'Hinc si V iam sit differentiale formae dV' matches the print (should logically be dU).
